name: Rostock
title: Thickness Gauging in Rostock: Ro-Pax, Tankers & Bulk Ships
description: Ship thickness measurement in Rostock and Warnemünde: UTM of ro-pax ferries, oil port tankers and bulk carriers, hull structure and ice-class gauging.
h1: Ultrasonic Gauging for Ferries, Tankers and Bulk Carriers in Rostock
intro: Rostock is eastern Germany's main seaport, with ro-pax ferries to Denmark and Sweden, an oil port feeding a pipeline to inland refining, bulk terminals for grain and fertiliser, and cruise calls at Warnemünde on the river mouth. Ships here range from ferries on tight crossings to tankers and bulk carriers whose holds and ballast tanks can be reached during a cargo call. Superintendents use us for thickness measurement in Rostock on those calls, and for each one a team travels out from India.

highlights.h: Baltic tankers at the oil port
highlights.p: Tankers using the Rostock oil port are typically Baltic-trading ships, often ice-classed. Deck structure, cargo-line supports and the ice-belt framing in the wing ballast tanks are measured under the terminal permit when those tanks can be entered safely.

Ferries on the Gedser and Trelleborg routes keep tight timetables. In-service gauging is limited to systems and spaces the crew can release; hull, car-deck and ramp structure is measured at refits or while a relief ship covers the route.

Grain, fertiliser and other bulk cargoes move through the overseas port on handysize and supramax ships. Hold, hatch coaming and topside tank gauging is planned for the period when holds are empty, before loading starts.

port.h: Rostock and Warnemünde: the port and its traffic
p: Rostock's seaport lies on the lower Warnow, with the Überseehafen on the east bank between the city and the Baltic, and Warnemünde at the river mouth. Rostock Port manages the overseas port, which combines a ferry and ro-ro terminal, an oil port, bulk terminals for grain, fertiliser and building materials, and heavy-lift quays used by the offshore wind and crane industries. Warnemünde handles the cruise ships, many of them using Rostock as the gateway for excursions to Berlin, and the Neptun Werft shipyard sits on the river at Warnemünde.

The ferries set the port's tempo. Ro-pax ships run to Gedser in Denmark and to Trelleborg in Sweden on frequent timetables, carrying cars, trucks and freight trailers, and they spend only short periods alongside between crossings. Cargo ships stay longer: a tanker at the oil port stays for its discharge, a bulk carrier for its loading or discharge, and project-cargo ships while heavy components are lifted aboard. Ships arriving ahead of their berth wait at anchor in the approaches off Warnemünde, and laid-up or off-hire ships lie at quays in the port.

Inspection demand reflects that mix and the Baltic setting. Ferries need hull, car-deck and ramp structure gauged at refits, with systems such as fire main and sea water piping checked between dockings. Tankers and bulk carriers trading in the Baltic are often ice-classed, so ice-belt plating and framing join the usual ESP or hull programme. Older tankers in Baltic trades, many owned or managed outside Germany, come under the same oil-major vetting and CAP requests as tankers anywhere, and a Rostock call can be a convenient place to answer them. Project-cargo and heavy-lift ships loading at the overseas port have crane-pedestal and heavy-deck structure that benefits from gauging and crack detection between voyages. Cruise ships at Warnemünde, by contrast, offer only their single port day.

facilities.h: Rostock berths and terminals where gauging is done
p: The oil port is the most regulated setting for tanker gauging in Rostock. Each tanker job is agreed with the terminal, and the team works under the ship's permit system with gas testing before any space is entered; cargo tanks are not entered during discharge. The bulk terminals give cleaner windows: a bulk carrier arriving in ballast to load grain or fertiliser has empty holds that can be gauged before loading starts, provided the ship can rig access and lighting. Heavy-lift quays see project-cargo ships whose cranes and decks are under particular load.

The ferry terminal in the overseas port handles both the passenger ferries and freight ro-ro ships. Short turnaround times limit what can be done in service, so substantial ro-pax ferry gauging is best scheduled during refits or when a ship is relieved by a spare vessel. At Warnemünde, cruise ships give single-day windows for narrowly defined piping and tank checks. Afloat repair work in the port is carried out by local contractors, and gauging can define the scope of such repairs before the work begins. Ships at the outer anchorages can be reached by launch, weather permitting, for small scopes.
list: Oil port, Überseehafen — deck, cargo-line support and ballast tank gauging on crude and product tankers during discharge, with gas testing and terminal permits.
Bulk terminals for grain and fertiliser — hold, hatch coaming and topside tank gauging on handysize and supramax bulkers before loading.
Ferry and ro-ro terminal — piping, void and car-deck gauging on ro-pax and freight ro-ro ships during longer stays or relief periods.
Heavy-lift and project quays — deck, crane pedestal and hatch structure gauging, with crack detection, on heavy-lift ships between voyages.
Warnemünde cruise terminal — a few flagged piping runs or tanks measured on a cruise ship during its port day.
Lay-by quays in the port — full hull, tank and deck programmes on laid-up or off-hire ships, including pre-purchase gauging.

context.h: Baltic regulation and the Rostock market
p: Rostock is a Paris MoU port within the Baltic Sea SOx ECA, where every ship calling must burn fuel of 0.10% sulphur or less or scrub its exhaust, and the Baltic ferry fleet has turned to scrubbers, compliant fuels and newer hybrid and alternative-fuel designs to meet it. Scrubber-fitted ferries and cargo ships should have their wash-water and overboard lines measured at each refit. Ships in the Baltic also follow ice-class requirements for winter trading to the northern Baltic, which brings ice-belt gauging into the planning for tankers and bulk carriers that go north in winter.

The oil port is a supply route for crude piped inland to the refinery at Schwedt, and the tankers using it are scrutinised by charterers and terminal vetting like any others. Grain exports from north-eastern Germany and fertiliser movements keep bulk carriers calling, and the offshore wind industry in the Baltic uses Rostock for components and service vessels. Baltic ferry operators, with fixed routes and heavy fuel use, feel the EU's carbon rules for shipping, ETS from 2024 and FuelEU Maritime a year later, more than most, and are weighing fleet renewal against keeping older tonnage in service for another survey cycle.

jobs.h: Gauging scopes typical of a Rostock call
jobs.p: Rostock work divides into cargo-call jobs on tankers and bulk carriers, where the cargo operation sets the window, and planned jobs on ferries and heavy-lift ships, which need the operator to set time aside. In both cases the scope is agreed in advance and the results reach the superintendent before the ship sails, so decisions on repairs or further gauging can be made before the next port. Examples:
list: An ice-class product tanker discharging at the oil port: deck plating, cargo-line supports and wing ballast tank ice-belt framing gauged during discharge, with cargo tanks deferred to the yard.
A supramax bulk carrier arriving in ballast to load grain at the Überseehafen: hold frames, hopper plating and hatch coamings gauged before loading begins.
A ro-pax ferry relieved by a spare ship: car-deck, ramp and shell gauging over a few days alongside, ahead of its renewal survey docking.
A heavy-lift ship loading crane components: crane pedestal and tween-deck structure gauging, with magnetic particle testing at pedestal welds, before the voyage.
A buyer's pre-purchase gauging of an ice-class bulk carrier laid up at a lay-by quay: holds, ballast tanks and ice-belt structure measured before the sale.

logistics: Hamburg and Berlin Brandenburg are the main international airports for Rostock, both connected by road and rail; Rostock-Laage handles a limited number of flights. Port areas and the cruise terminal are ISPS-controlled, and the oil port adds its own safety induction, so the agent registers the team and its equipment before the ship berths. The team from India must hold Schengen visas to enter Germany; the earlier we know the call or refit date, the more reliably we can line up visas, flights and the terminal paperwork.

faqs.q: Our ferry is about to be relieved for refit. Can you gauge it in Rostock first?
faqs.a: Yes, and the days between relief and the yard are often the best gauging window a ferry gets. With the ship out of service at a Rostock quay, the team can cover car decks, ramps, door surroundings and ballast tanks, mark plates near their renewal limit, and hand the superintendent a steel estimate before the refit specification is final.

faqs.q: Do ice-class tankers need anything extra gauged?
faqs.a: Yes. Ice-belt plating and the frames and stringers behind it need their own attention, because ice abrasion and impact add to corrosion there. From inside the wing ballast tanks, the team can measure ice-belt plating and framing alongside the normal ESP programme, so the superintendent sees the ice-strengthened structure as a distinct item before the winter season.

faqs.q: Can you work at the Warnemünde cruise terminal?
faqs.a: Yes, within the narrow window of a cruise call. The technical team usually flags specific systems or tanks, the security officer arranges access in line with the ship's security plan, and the work is planned so that it finishes before passengers return or embarkation begins. Larger programmes are kept for the ship's dry-docking.

faqs.q: Can one mobilisation cover Rostock and other Baltic ports?
faqs.a: Yes. A team in Rostock can move on to Kiel, the Danish and Swedish ferry ports or ports further east, if the dates line up and visas cover the countries involved. Most of the Baltic coast is within the Schengen area, which simplifies multi-port work, and we plan the sequence around each ship's schedule.
